extra.message: Hardcoded weak JWT signing secret — Attacker forges JWTs for arbitrary user_ids (including admin), bypassing authentication entirely. [verified: auth.py:23 decodes JWTs with hardcoded key 'secret' and auth_routes.py:48 signs with the same 'secret' using HS256, so an attacker can trivially forge a token for any user_id (e.g. admin) and bypass authentication.]

SQL injection in register via username — Attacker can inject SQL to corrupt/insert arbitrary rows, manipulate balances, or read data via stacked/sub queries; full DB compromise. [verified: register() interpolates JSON `username` directly into an f-string INSERT executed via db.session.execute with no parameterization or escaping; unauthenticated attacker controls the value.]

SQL injection in login via username — Authentication bypass and arbitrary data extraction from the user table (hashes, PII) by an unauthenticated attacker. [verified: login() builds `SELECT * FROM user WHERE username = '{username}'` from unauthenticated input and executes it raw, enabling auth-bypass/data extraction via injection.]

SQL injection / IDOR in get_transactions via user_id query param — Authenticated attacker reads any user's full transaction history and can inject arbitrary SQL to dump the entire database. [verified: get_transactions interpolates request.args.get('user_id') directly into f-string SQL (line 51) with no parameterization, and token_required only authenticates without ownership checks; both SQLi and IDOR are reachable by any authenticated user.]

Reflected CORS origin with credentials enabled — Any website can issue credentialed cross-origin requests, enabling theft of profile/transaction data and CSRF-like actions on behalf of a logged-in victim. [verified: Same after_request handler reads the Origin header and reflects it with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true; the insecure CORS setting is genuinely present, enabling credentialed cross-origin data theft and CSRF-like actions.]

Reflected CORS origin with credentials allowed — Any malicious website can make authenticated cross-origin requests on behalf of a logged-in victim, reading balances/PII and initiating transfers. [verified: after_request reflects request Origin into Access-Control-Allow-Origin (app.py ~L53) while setting Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true (~L56), allowing any site to make credentialed cross-origin requests to read PII/balances and act on the victim's behalf.]

Flask debug mode enabled in production run — Exposed Werkzeug debugger can allow RCE; verbose tracebacks leak source/config to attackers. [verified: app.run(host='0.0.0.0', debug=True, port=5000) enables the Werkzeug interactive debugger on all interfaces, and error handlers return str(error) leaking internals; this is genuinely present and reachable on the run path.]

Sensitive PII (SSN) stored and exposed in plaintext — User SSNs and other PII are stored unencrypted and exposed via the API/DB, enabling identity theft if accessed (e.g. via the IDOR/SQLi findings). [verified: Profile JSON (seeded with 'ssn' in app.py) is stored plaintext in User.profile Text column and returned verbatim by /api/me via current_user.get_profile(), exposing SSN/DOB/address/phone unencrypted (CWE-312).]

Weak unsalted MD5 password hashing in registration — If the database is leaked, attacker can crack all user passwords nearly instantly due to fast unsalted MD5, enabling account takeover and credential reuse. [verified: register() at line 21 computes hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest() with no salt and stores it; MD5 is fast and unsalted, so a DB leak allows trivial offline cracking of all passwords (CWE-916 weak hash, control genuinely absent).]

Hardcoded/weak JWT signing secret — Attacker can forge JWTs for any user (including admin), bypassing authentication entirely and accessing/transferring any account's funds. [verified: JWTs are signed with the hardcoded literal 'secret' in login() and verified with the same 'secret' in auth.py jwt.decode, so any attacker can forge tokens for any user_id.]

Password reset for arbitrary user via client-supplied user_id (IDOR) — Full account takeover of any user (including admin) by resetting their password; attacker gains access to balances, PII and funds. [verified: Duplicate of the update-password IDOR: backend reads `user_id` from the body and resets that user's password with no ownership check, enabling account takeover.]

IDOR: change any user's password by arbitrary user_id — Full account takeover of any user (including admins) by an authenticated attacker who supplies a target user_id. [verified: update_password() reads `user_id` from the body and calls User.query.get(user_id).set_password() with no check against current_user.id, allowing any authenticated user to take over any account.]

Insecure YAML deserialization leading to RCE — Remote code execution on the server as the Flask process; full host/database compromise. [verified: Duplicate YAML deserialization finding: /api/profile/import uses yaml.load with the full yaml.Loader on attacker JSON, allowing arbitrary Python object construction / RCE.]

Missing amount validation enables negative-amount transfer theft — Authenticated attacker steals money from arbitrary accounts by transferring a negative amount. [verified: transfer only checks current_user.balance < amount with no positivity validation; a negative amount passes the check and 'balance -= amount' inflates sender while 'receiver.balance += amount' drains the receiver, enabling theft.]

Negative/unvalidated transfer amount allows balance inflation — Attacker can send a negative amount to steal funds from another account and inflate their own balance arbitrarily. [verified: Duplicate of finding 2: no positivity validation on amount, so a negative transfer passes the balance check and increases the sender's balance while reducing the receiver's, allowing balance inflation/theft.]

IDOR: read any user's transactions via user_id query parameter — Any authenticated user can enumerate and read other users' transaction records (amounts, counterparties, descriptions), breaching confidentiality of all users' financial activity. [verified: user_id is taken from the query string (line 48) and used to fetch transactions with no check that it equals current_user.id; token_required performs only authentication, so any authenticated user reads others' transaction history.]

SQL injection via description in transaction search — Authenticated attacker can extract arbitrary data (password hashes, SSNs, JWT-relevant data) or manipulate the DB through UNION/boolean/time-based injection. [verified: Duplicate of finding 1: the 'description' query param is concatenated into raw SQL LIKE with no parameterization; URL-decoded metacharacters reach the query enabling injection.]

Hardcoded weak Flask SECRET_KEY — Predictable signing key undermines any Flask signing/session integrity; attacker can forge signed values. [verified: app.config['SECRET_KEY']='supersecret' (app.py L16) is a hardcoded weak secret reachable on every run, securing any Flask signing/session functionality; severity is medium since no Flask session cookies are actively used (db.session refs are SQLAlchemy, JWT uses a separate literal).]

Weak unsalted MD5 password hashing — If the DB is exposed (e.g. via the SQLi above), passwords are recovered almost instantly, enabling credential reuse and account takeover. [verified: models.py:24 set_password uses hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest() with no salt; check_password compares the same way, so stored credentials are fast/unsalted and trivially crackable if the DB is exposed (CWE-916).]

Missing brute-force protection on login/register — Attacker can brute-force passwords (weak MD5/common passwords) and enumerate accounts without restriction. [verified: login()/register() have no lockout or throttling; LoginAttempt rows are written but never queried to block repeated failures, leaving brute-force unrestricted.]

Sensitive PII (SSN) exposure in profile responses and at rest — SSN and other PII are exposed in API responses and stored in plaintext, enabling identity theft if accessed via XSS/SQLi/CORS. [verified: /api/me returns current_user.get_profile() which includes the plaintext ssn/dob seeded in app.py, and the data is stored unencrypted; combined with SQLi/CORS this exposes PII.]

Race condition in transfer balance check — Attacker can spend more than their balance (double-spend) via concurrent transfer requests. [verified: Balance is verified via check-then-act (line 31) with SQLite isolation_level=None and no row locking (app.py), so concurrent transfers can both pass the check before either commits, allowing overdraft/double-spend.]

JWT stored in localStorage (token theft exposure) — Any XSS or malicious script can read and exfiltrate the bearer token, leading to full account takeover; tokens cannot be revoked server-side. [verified: App.js line 53 does localStorage.setItem('token', data.token) and reads it via localStorage.getItem('token') in fetchUserData, Header, Dashboard, and Profile, so the JWT is exposed to any JavaScript and exfiltrable via XSS; logout is client-side only and tokens are long-lived/non-revocable per the threat model, confirming the CWE-522 weakness. Severity is medium since exploitation requires a separ]

Username enumeration on registration — An attacker can enumerate valid account usernames, aiding targeted credential-stuffing and phishing against known customers. [verified: register() returns the distinct 400 'Username already exists' only when the username matches, allowing unauthenticated enumeration of valid usernames.]

Missing input validation on registration — Malformed requests cause 500 errors (leaking via error handler) and allow weak/empty credentials; contributes to the SQLi sink. [verified: register() calls password.encode() without checking presence, so a missing password raises an unhandled AttributeError surfaced as a 500; no field validation exists.]
